title: Recent research at Cambridge on radial basis functions
contribution: Status report (DAMTP 1998/NA05) on three Cambridge RBF topics: a fast iterative solver for thin-plate-spline interpolation with n up to 10^5, an RBF semi-norm criterion for choosing the next point in expensive global optimization, and numerically observed edge-accuracy orders of 1-D thin-plate splines.
problem_entry: Numerical facts: dense TPS systems need O(n log n) iterations for n > 10^4 (pp. 3, 7); experiments show accuracy orders not confirmed by theory (p. 3); Jones (1996) prompts RBF-based global optimization of expensive f (p. 8).
key_idea: Newton-form interpolation with approximate Lagrange functions on q ≈ 30 nearest points plus iterative refinement (pp. 4–7); choose x_{n+1} by minimising the semi-norm of the interpolant through a target value f*, closed form (3.27) (pp. 8–13); change side conditions to raise edge accuracy while keeping scaling invariance (pp. 15–17).
assumptions: P full rank (non-collinear points for d = 2 TPS) and conditionally positive definite φ (p. 2); expensive derivative-free f in §3 (p. 8); uniform 1-D grid and smooth f in §4 (pp. 13–14).
proof_devices: minimum semi-norm property of RBF interpolation via conditional positive definiteness after padding the centre set with zero coefficients, (3.10)–(3.15) (pp. 10–11)
orthogonality of the new Lagrange function to the current interpolant gives a closed-form merit σ̂(x, f*) (3.24)–(3.27) (p. 13)
scaling-invariance check (4.10)–(4.12) used to reject/repair a variant (pp. 16–17)
experiments: Halving tables of |e(h/2)| for n = 80–640 under several f and side conditions (Tables 1–3, pp. 14–16); constructed divergence cases for the cheaper iterative variant (n = 1000 on two concentric quarter circles, p. 7).
positioning: Builds on Beatson–Powell 1992/1994, Powell 1997, Duchon 1977, Schaback 1993 and Jones 1996 without criticising anyone (pp. 3, 8, 9, 12).
writing: Group status report with open questions marked open (pp. 1, 7, 14) and precise acknowledgement of each student's contribution (p. 17).
limits_future: Fast variant fails on constructed examples, intermediate version under study (p. 7); global-optimization algorithms only hoped for (p. 9); edge orders are conjectures (pp. 14–15); best 1-D variant not recommended over cubic splines (p. 17).

title: Proof of convergence of an iterative technique for thin plate spline interpolation in two dimensions
contribution: Proves convergence of (a generalisation of) the Beatson–Goodsell–Powell iterative thin-plate-spline solver by showing every stage reduces the native semi-norm of the error, and extends the result to conditionally positive/negative definite radial functions.
problem_entry: A method that worked in practice (p. 7) lacked a proof; the direct O(n^3) solve is prohibitive for n > 1000 (p. 3) and the spectral-radius route was thought very hard (p. 4).
key_idea: Each stage adds a multiple of an approximate Lagrange function on q points, like forward substitution, and a final stage interpolates the last q residuals (pp. 3–4); the step coefficient equals the exact minimiser of (s*−s, s*−s) along that function (p. 5).
assumptions: Distinct, non-collinear data points and non-collinear L_k\{k} (p. 3); for the extension, conditional definiteness of order m, q > dim Π_m, L_k\{k} not in a polynomial zero set (pp. 7–8).
proof_devices: native-norm descent: each stage is an exact line search in the semi-norm, shown by integration by parts (3.1)–(3.2) (p. 5)
last stage as orthogonal projection onto a subspace (3.4) (p. 5)
monotone bounded sequence ⇒ inner products → 0 via identity (3.6), then induction and back-substitution through a triangular system with nonzero diagonal (3.9) (p. 6)
finite dimension ⇒ equivalence of norms, norm = max over data points (3.5) (p. 6)
experiments: Circle, grid, random disc and a deliberately slow case D (two concentric eighth-circles, radii 1 and 1+10^-5), n = 400/900, q = 10–50, tolerance 10^-8, iteration counts beside the largest normalised scalar product (5.1), including runs stopped at 1000 iterations (p. 9).
positioning: Contrasts with the spectral-radius approach of Beatson, Goodsell and Powell (1995) (pp. 4–5); credits Beatson with the original idea and Goodsell with the programs (p. 10).
writing: Short proof-centred paper; the expectation linking speed to orthogonality is stated before the experiments (p. 9).
limits_future: Convergence without a rate; the observed link between speed and orthogonality ((5.1) < 0.1) is offered to guide the choice of L_k (p. 10).

title: Krylov subspace methods for radial basis function interpolation
contribution: Recasts the Cambridge iterative RBF solvers as a Krylov subspace method in the native semi-norm, gives four sufficient conditions on the operator A for exact-arithmetic termination, specifies a recommended A from approximate Lagrange functions, and measures when the Krylov safeguard pays.
problem_entry: Direct solves limit n to about 1000 (p. 4); Goodsell's cheaper method occasionally fails to converge, so a Krylov technique was added and then reinterpreted as the core (p. 5).
key_idea: Iterate k is the element of span{A^j s*} closest to s* in the native semi-norm, computed CG-style (pp. 8–9) using ⟨s, s*⟩ obtainable from the data (2.6) (p. 7); A built from approximate Lagrange functions on q ≈ 30 nearest points plus an exact q-point operator H, aiming at A ≈ I (pp. 14–16).
assumptions: Distinct, polynomially unisolvent points; conditionally definite φ with sign σ (pp. 3–4); for TPS three far-from-collinear points forced into every L_j (p. 22).
proof_devices: sufficient-condition abstraction: nonsingularity, polynomial reproduction, ellipticity, self-adjointness (3.6) (p. 9)
induction giving conjugacy, strict semi-norm decrease and termination in ≤ n − m̂ + 1 iterations (pp. 10–12)
Gram–Schmidt direction (3.21) when A is not self-adjoint (pp. 12–13)
greatest-index argument for ellipticity of the recommended A (4.19)–(4.20) (p. 17)
experiments: Circle, grid, random disc and two arcs 10^-5 apart; random data, ε = 10^-8, n = 400/900, q = 10/30/50, φ = r and r² log r; iteration counts (Tables 2–3, p. 21), comparison with the plain iteration governed by the spectral radius of I − A (p. 21), random orderings (p. 23).
positioning: Like GMRES but A need not come from the equations and the semi-norm need not be a norm (p. 8); follows Dyn–Levin–Rippa CG and Beatson–Powell 1994 (p. 5).
writing: Calls its own termination proof misleading about practice (p. 13) and narrates how each test problem shaped the algorithm (pp. 19–20).
limits_future: Guarantee plus large gains in hard cases at O(n) extra work (p. 22), but little advantage on most problems (p. 22); open: slow TPS Problem 4, ordering, d ≥ 3; software promised after that work (pp. 22–23).

title: An optimal way of moving a sequence of points onto a curve in two dimensions
contribution: Gives an algorithm that finds the global lexicographic minimax assignment of ordered points to parameters on a piecewise arc/segment curve, usually in O(n) total work, using greedy feasibility sweeps, bisection on the optimal value and splitting by certified bounds.
problem_entry: Application pull from image registration (initial values for mapping curves into curves, Powell 1996), with local minima from a self-intersecting curve (pp. 2–3).
key_idea: A greedy forward/backward sweep decides h ≥ h* or h < h* (Lemma 1, Corollary 2, pp. 4–5); bisection on h yields certified bounds on each t*_i that split the problem into independent subproblems (Lemmas 3, 4, 6, pp. 5–10).
assumptions: Curve of circular arcs and straight segments with continuous direction (pp. 2–3); analysis valid in higher dimensions (p. 11); bracket tolerance at least h0 times relative machine precision (p. 12).
proof_devices: greedy sweep + induction for a feasibility oracle (Lemma 1, p. 4)
exchange argument for splitting, proved formally though obvious (Lemma 3, p. 5)
exact optimality of a cheap choice for a perturbed problem with perturbation equal to the bracket width (Lemma 5, (2.8), pp. 7–8)
experiments: Rounded-hexagon curves (1 or n/125 cycles), n = 125–8000, perturbations 0/δ/10δ, CPU seconds (Table 1, p. 22); constructed O(n²) case (Table 2, pp. 23–24); accuracy check by solving the reversed problem (p. 25).
positioning: Minimax objective set against a sum-of-squares formulation (p. 3); image-registration literature for motivation (p. 2).
writing: Surprisingly small errors called incredible, then explained by a hypothesis checked with extra program output (pp. 25–26).
limits_future: O(n²) work for data far from the curve (pp. 23–24), theoretical ε^{1/2} accuracy of the bisection route (p. 25), no known application needing high accuracy (p. 26); further analytic techniques proposed (p. 26).

title: On the convergence of the DFP algorithm for unconstrained optimization when there are only two variables
contribution: Proves that DFP with exact (first-local-minimum, monotone) line searches has gradients not bounded away from zero for any C² function of two variables with bounded level sets, without convexity.
problem_entry: DFP convergence theory since ~1970 assumed convexity (p. 2); Powell seeks theorems or counterexamples under bounded level sets and C² (p. 2), to explain DFP's success rather than improve software (p. 3).
key_idea: For n = 2 the exact line search and quasi-Newton equation fix the next direction by (1.5), so B_k disappears from the analysis (p. 3); comparison with Polak–Ribière counterexamples isolates monotone line-search decrease as the needed hypothesis (pp. 3–4).
assumptions: n = 2, bounded level set, continuous second derivatives (1.1), step to the largest α with monotone decrease (pp. 2–3); no convexity (p. 1).
proof_devices: reduction of the algorithm to direction conditions in the smallest case n = 2 (p. 3)
topology of the limit set T of the piecewise-linear iterate path: closed, connected, no stationary points, collinear (Lemmas 2.1–2.4, pp. 5–8)
Zoutendijk-type bound Σcos²θ_k < ∞ (2.7) (p. 7)
WLOG normalisation of T to a unit segment (pp. 8–9)
sign split of iterations into K_same/K_opp and monotone ‖d_k‖/‖g_k‖ on K_opp contradicting ‖d_k‖ → ∞ (pp. 9–10)
positioning: Builds on Powell 1972 (Theorem 2), Dixon 1972, Wolfe 1970 and Powell's 1984 CG counterexamples (pp. 2–4, 7).
writing: Personal dedication to Davidon (p. 2); intricate lemma isolated with advice to read §4 first (pp. 4, 10); closes by calling the result a small contribution (p. 22).
limits_future: Only n = 2; for n ≥ 3 the path can pass around T (p. 22); an n = 3 counterexample sought with Dai as a nonlinear feasibility problem, unsuccessful for months, paper deferred (pp. 22–23).

title: Radial basis function methods for interpolation to functions of many variables
contribution: Reviews RBF interpolation theory and shows numerically that, for data on 2- or 3-dimensional nonlinear manifolds in R^d with d up to 40, linear and multiquadric interpolation accuracy and the iteration counts of the Cambridge solver are nearly independent of d.
problem_entry: Fixed basis spaces become singular for some point positions when d ≥ 2 (p. 2); data-mining data (e.g. life expectancy from d answers) lie near low-dimensional manifolds, so does needed n depend on d? (pp. 1, 6).
key_idea: Review of nonsingularity, polynomial terms and grid accuracy (pp. 2–6), then experiments on synthetic edge-free nonlinear manifolds using the Faul–Goodsell–Powell CG-like solver (pp. 7–13, 17–19).
assumptions: Linear or multiquadric φ with a constant (p. 7); Gaussian test f with width set by min f(x_i) = 0.01 (p. 7); manifolds built from distorted sines with random phases (pp. 7–8).
proof_devices: review-level nonsingularity via conditional negative definiteness (p. 3)
regular-simplex counterexample for TPS without polynomial term (p. 4)
experiments: Accuracy for d = 5–40, n = 64–4096, grids with/without edges, random points, c > 0 (Tables 1–4, pp. 8–12); iteration counts for q = 10/30/50, tolerance 10^-8 (Tables 5–6, pp. 18–19).
positioning: Draws on Hardy, Micchelli, Buhmann, Bejancu (pp. 2–6); acknowledges fast multipole methods missing from his code (p. 21).
writing: Concrete application example motivates manifolds (p. 6); explicit caveats on random-point figures (p. 10); surprises flagged (p. 18).
limits_future: √n iteration growth for random data in the ball with d ≥ 5 (p. 18), more iterations for multiquadrics (p. 19), slow beyond 5000 points on a Sparc 10 (p. 21), attempted improvement gave the same coefficients (p. 22); Fortran program available (p. 22).

title: A Krylov subspace algorithm for multiquadric interpolation in many dimensions
contribution: Specifies and analyses the Faul–Goodsell–Powell preconditioned-CG (Krylov) solver for multiquadric interpolation in any dimension, proving termination, a linear rate governed by a spectral radius, and optimality of its Lagrange-function coefficients, with extensive randomised experiments for d = 2–40 and n up to 10000.
problem_entry: Earlier Cambridge solvers need about ten iterations for d = 2, c = 0 but lose efficiency as d and c grow; convergence to be guaranteed (p. 1); fast multipole hard for d > 3 (p. 3).
key_idea: Random ordering, nearest-q sets with an exchange rule, Cholesky-based approximate Lagrange functions, CG-like directions and a max-residual-minimising constant (Steps 0–9, pp. 3–6), read as preconditioned CG with Ξ ≈ Ξfull (pp. 3, 16).
assumptions: Distinct points, c ≥ 0, Micchelli's negative definiteness of Φ on zero-sum vectors (pp. 2, 9).
proof_devices: Krylov termination/conjugacy theorem by induction (Theorem 1, p. 13)
linear rate by substituting (I − Ξ)^k into the Krylov minimum; ρ = spectral radius of I − H for a normalised Gram matrix (pp. 18–19)
expected-cost analysis of set construction under random ordering (3.3)–(3.4) (pp. 7–8)
optimality theorem closing a proposed improvement via Cauchy–Schwarz and orthogonal decomposition (Theorem 2, pp. 21–23)
experiments: Problems A–D, n = 200–10000, q = 10–50, ε = 10^-10, ten random instances with min–max ranges (Table 1, p. 24); d = 5–40 (Table 2, p. 26); c > 0 averages (Table 3, p. 27); timings vs direct method on a Sun Ultra 10 (Table 4, p. 28).
positioning: Continues Beatson–Powell 1994, Powell 1997, Faul–Powell 2000, Faul 2001, Powell 2002; ~25% more iterations than Powell 1997 except q = 10 (pp. 2–3, 25).
writing: Specification first, reasons later (p. 3); unexplained findings reported as unexplained after a designed test (p. 26).
limits_future: Iterations nearly proportional to n for d = 40, c > 0 (p. 27); q choice application-dependent (p. 28); one nonpositive Cholesky pivot run replaced (pp. 24–25); free Fortran 77 code, up to 10000 points (p. 29).

title: Fast evaluation of polyharmonic splines in three dimensions
contribution: Derives far-field expansions, error bounds, a uniqueness lemma and translation formulae for (ν+1)-harmonic splines in R³ and details a binary-tree hierarchical evaluator that computes matrix–vector products in O(N log N).
problem_entry: O(N) per evaluation and O(N²) per matrix–vector product bottleneck iterative interpolation (citing Faul–Goodsell–Powell) and applications such as lidar surface reconstruction and ore grade modelling (pp. 2, 19).
key_idea: Generalised Legendre expansion (Theorem 4.1, p. 9) with truncation bound (Theorem 4.2, p. 12); uniqueness of truncated outer expansions lets parent coefficients come cheaply from children (pp. 14, 17); hierarchical tree with per-panel distance thresholds per truncation order (pp. 18–22).
assumptions: Distinct centres unisolvent for π_ν (p. 2); real coefficients for symmetry savings (p. 23).
proof_devices: coefficients found by algebra for ν = 1–4, then proved generally (Iserles; later authors' induction) (p. 12)
uniqueness lemma for truncated expansions used to certify indirect computation (Lemma 5.1, pp. 14, 17)
adaptive error estimate with three safety layers of coefficients (§7.1, pp. 22–23)
experiments: Biharmonic matrix–vector products, N = 4000–128000, centres in a cube or on a sphere, relative accuracy 10^-3/10^-6, 10 replications, fast vs direct times (Tables 1–2, pp. 24–25).
positioning: Builds on Barnes–Hut, Greengard–Rokhlin, Epton–Dembart and Powell's 1993 2-D TPS evaluator (pp. 3, 19).
writing: States the engineering choice plainly: hierarchical code because it is much simpler and full FMM wins only for very large N (p. 27).
limits_future: Adaptive error estimate could fail for contrived data (p. 23); per-panel tolerance heuristic (p. 23); extra log N vs full FMM (p. 27); outer-to-inner formulas given for a future full FMM (pp. 27–28).
